/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.headline: UK households have paid extra £13,961 on bills since 2021 amid soaring inflation, TUC says
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.excerpt: UK households have paid almost £14,000 on average in additional costs for mortgages, loans, energy and water bills over the past five years, according to a report urging the chancellor to tackle soaring living costs at the budget. With less than a fortnight before John Healey’s first budget as chancellor, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) said the cost of living crisis was weighing on the economy as hard-pressed households held back on spending. Urging the chancellor to support households through a series of measures in the budget, it said the UK had recorded the weakest growth in consumer spending in the G7 since before the pandemic. According to analysis of official figures by the union umbrella body, British households have forked out an additional £13,961 on bills on average since 2021 – an extra £2,792 a year – amid soaring inflation triggered by the exit from the Covid pandemic and wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said: “From austerity to the pandemic to energy shocks and Trumpflation, working people have borne the brunt of crisis after crisis. When the crackpots in the White House or the Kremlin launch an illegal war, everyone pays the price in their bills.” In his speech at Labour’s conference in Liverpool, Healey pledged to use his 28 October budget to give households “breathing space”. However, he warned that the government had limited resources to soften the global economic shock hitting Britain.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.trail: Trades Union Congress urges chancellor to tackle rising additional living costs in this month’s budget

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.headline: John Healey ‘targets tax crackdown on online marketplaces’ in first budget
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.excerpt: A tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could raise up to £1bn more for the Treasury is reportedly being drawn up for John Healey’s first budget. The chancellor is said to be preparing to announce that online marketplaces will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by all retailers selling on their platforms. Marketplaces have been required to collect VAT for overseas businesses selling into the UK since 2021 but some foreign operators have posed as British retailers, using shell companies or other techniques to avoid this rule. Under the proposed change, websites would be made responsible for collecting VAT at source for retailers on their platform who have an annual turnover of more than £90,000, no matter where they are based. Healey is expected to announce this change will be made to fund cuts to business rates for high street shops, the Times reported. The government ran a consultation over the summer on changing the “deemed reseller” rules, saying “non-compliance persists among both overseas and UK-based businesses, distorting competition and disadvantaging compliant firms online and on the high street”. It consulted food delivery platforms as well as retail marketplaces, suggesting it was considering drawing them into the system. Amazon said it welcomed the prospect of a change to deemed reseller rules.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.trail: Move aimed at firms such as Amazon and eBay could raise up to £1bn more for Treasury, says report

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.headline: UK high street bosses urge chancellor to cut cost of employing young people
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.excerpt: Some of the UK’s biggest retailers and hospitality businesses, including Tesco, Costa Coffee and the Co-op, have met John Healey to urge him to cut the cost of employing young people in his first budget. At the No 11 event on Tuesday morning, the chancellor heard from sector leaders – including the boss of Marks & Spencer, Stuart Machin, and Sainsbury’s chief executive, Simon Roberts – about the impact of the rise in employers’ national insurance contributions (Nics). Businesses want a partial reversal of the surprise move by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, who lowered the earnings threshold at which they start to pay Nics from £9,100 to £5,000 a year. They argue the change contributed to the plunge in the number of high street jobs for young people and part-time workers and a rise in youth unemployment. They want the Nics threshold raised to £6,000, arguing this would help create jobs and ease inflation pressures on high streets. Retail and hospitality firms also hope Healey will ease the burden of business rates, and one source close to the meeting said they were optimistic on both fronts. “It felt like they were listening,” the source said. Healey has vowed to ease the cost of doing business amid mounting pressures on firms from rising energy bills.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.trail: Retailers call on John Healey to raise national insurance contributions threshold in his first budget

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.headline: ‘If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we’re screwed’: Labour insiders voice fears over budget
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.excerpt: In the days since Labour’s annual conference, party insiders have been sharing a word cloud produced by the pollsters More in Common, which shows the phrases voters most associate with Andy Burnham. Such polling is rarely flattering for politicians, and the prime minister’s version had its fair share of negatives. But one of the most prominent words in the cloud – and the one that has caught the imagination of Labour strategists – was “trying”. At a cabinet away day at Chequers on Monday and a meeting for special advisers on Thursday, the idea that the government was doing its best to improve people’s lives – despite the difficult economic backdrop – was a golden thread. “The public think the only person that can reach those levers is you,” said a government insider. “They justifiably ask, can you do it or not? And if not, they’ll look for an alternative. We have to avoid the sense of things being out of our control.” A party strategist said: “Voters don’t want us to put our hands up in despair; they want us to roll our sleeves up. They don’t want us to be helpless in the face of global stuff; they want answers.” But will this prime minister be able to provide them? At conference, Burnham set out his big vision for the future – on social care and the pensions triple lock, the EU and electoral reform. The party faithful lapped it up and polling suggested the “Burnham bounce” had continued.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.trail: Some say party risks ‘looking twee’ by focusing on small fixes amid growing nervousness that budget lacks ambition

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.headline: Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.excerpt: Tax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues, according to campaigners, who are calling on the chancellor, John Healey, to increase taxes and force lenders to pay their “fair share” in the budget. Calculations by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents unions with more than 5.3 million members across England and Wales, shows that the public purse is billions of pounds worse off as a result of tax cuts introduced under the Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt in 2023. The then government agreed to slash the bank surcharge – an additional levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% that year. The move was meant to offset a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%, after the industry argued higher taxes would put them at a competitive disadvantage compared with other big financial centres such as New York. However, the cuts came just as lenders started reaping handsome earnings, thanks to rising interest rates. The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have now generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years. The TUC says the 2023 cuts ultimately robbed the UK purse of tax revenues. Its analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the UK public lost out £2.3bn in 2023-24, a further £1.7bn in 2024-25, and £2bn in 2025-26 – totalling £6bn over three years. With banks pocketing record profits, the TUC said the surcharge should now be increased beyond its pre-2023 level at the 28 October budget.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/john-healey-raise-t.trail: Exclusive: Chancellor urged to reverse Jeremy Hunt’s tax surcharge cuts to claw back billions in lost revenue

/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.headline: No signs Chagos deal can be adapted to suit Trump, say UK officials
/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.excerpt: The Chagos Islands deal is on hold for as long as Donald Trump objects to it, UK officials believe, with no immediate signs it can be adapted to suit the US president. After Trump savaged the three-way plan as “a terrible deal” during a meeting with Andy Burnham at the UN general assembly, the prime minister said he was “confident” the UK would be able to find a solution to revive the idea. But while efforts are still taking place to do this, there is an acceptance in the government that it is extremely unlikely unless Trump has another change of heart. “Until the president changes his mind there will not be any progress,” one official said. “We are where we are. We were waiting for the president to present a view, which he has.” The UK signed a treaty last year to transfer sovereignty over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, while retaining control of the joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia, part of the Indian Ocean archipelago, under a 99-year lease. Mauritius was set to receive £165m for three years and £120m a year from the fourth year. Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said on Wednesday morning that payments worth at least £120m to Mauritius were on hold given the deal could not go ahead without US support. “This deal as it is currently constituted can’t go ahead without American support,” Streeting told BBC Radio 4’s Today’s programme.
/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.trail: Agreement with Mauritius over Diego Garcia unlikely to be revived unless president changes his mind, insiders believe

/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.headline: UK to give support to Saudi jets in attempt to counter Houthi fighters
/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.excerpt: The UK has agreed to provide defensive air support to Saudi Arabia to help counter Houthi fighters and restore stability in the Middle East while driving down the cost of living at home, Andy Burnham has said, ahead of his first meeting with Donald Trump. The prime minister said he had agreed to a request for air-to-air refuelling of Saudi jets to defend energy infrastructure against the Iran-backed rebels and help keep oil flowing from the Gulf to ease global economic turmoil. Burnham also revealed he will use his first meeting with Trump on Tuesday to urge the US president to de-escalate the conflict in Iran, warning that “dark clouds of global instability” are directly affecting people’s lives all over the world. The turmoil in the Middle East has pushed up global energy prices, putting the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and increasing government borrowing costs to multi-year highs just weeks before a crucial first budget for the new government. On the flight to the United Nations in New York, Burnham told reporters that an RAF Voyager would help refuel Saudi jets for several weeks, in his first military deployment since taking power, after the Houthis advanced to areas adjacent to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait. The key Gulf ally has used the waterway as an alternative route for oil exports bypassing disruption in the ⁠strait of Hormuz. The RAF operational support is in addition to the UK Sky Sabre air defence system already operating.
/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.trail: Andy Burnham seeks stability in Middle East to bring down prices at home as first meeting with Trump looms

/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.headline: UK hits back at Argentinian Falklands claim and insists islands remain British
/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.excerpt: British ministers have hit back after the Argentinian president said “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the Falklands were “blowing around the world”. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the UK would “resolutely uphold” the self-determination of the islands after the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, said his country needed to take them back. Miliband said in a post on X: “The UK’s position on the Falkland Islands is unwavering. The islands are British and will remain so because that is the overwhelming position of the Islanders. “Their right of self-determination is paramount, grounded in international law and we will resolutely uphold it.” Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said Milei’s statement “tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands”. He added on X: “The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British. Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable.” Lucy Powell, the education secretary, also insisted the islands were British, adding: “We will defend the right of those who live in the Falkland Islands to determine their own future.” The latest diplomatic spat over the south Atlantic archipelago came after comments by the US president, Donald Trump, who has cast doubt on American support for British control of the islands. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the Falklands’ sovereignty, while recognising Britain’s de facto control over them.
/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.trail: Ed Miliband says Britain’s position remains ‘unwavering’ in response to remarks by Argentina’s president

/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.headline: What is behind Russia’s ‘consequences’ threat over UK sending drones to Ukraine?
/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.excerpt: Russia’s embassy in London has accused the UK of “deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis, while hypocritically professing a desire for peace” after it emerged over the weekend that Britain was supplying attack drones to Kyiv. What has the UK done – and what was Russia’s response? Ministry of Defence sources indicated that a report in the Sunday Times, that two drones made by British companies had been used by Ukraine’s military to attack targets inside Russia, was true, although only one, Nyan, made by BAE Systems, was named. The Russian embassy, seeking to maximise the impact of its remarks, added in a widely reported statement on Telegram: “London’s actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer”. Is the UK’s drone supply actually an escalation? Britain has been supplying weapons and providing financial support to Ukraine since before Russia’s full-scale invasion. It has committed to providing £3bn a year in military aid until the end of the decade and to joining the EU’s €90bn loan scheme, which bankrolls Kyiv’s military effort, though many of the details of UK support are kept secret. The £100,000 Nyan drone is a medium-sized, jet-powered delta wing drone capable of delivering relatively small attacks at distances greater than 150 miles. However, while it looks hi-tech, it is not a munition that appears to be militarily significant.
/politics/2026/oct/15/wes-streeting-us-s.trail: Britain has supplied more militarily significant munitions to Kyiv before but there are political reasons for Moscow’s remarks

/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.headline: Caribbean nations draft action plan to push UK to redress reparations over slavery
/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.excerpt: Caribbean nations are drawing up a multi-pronged “action plan” with legal options to push the UK into negotiating a decades-long slavery reparations deal, officials at a reparations conference have said. Leaders in the region are hoping the UK would agree to targeted and constructive negotiation talks at upcoming Commonwealth and UN summits, but they are ready to take the matter to international courts if Britain continues to resist diplomatic options. Earlier this month, a spokesperson for Andy Burnham reiterated the British government’s long‑held position that “the UK does not and will not pay reparations”. Ralph Gonsalves, the former prime minister of St Vincent and the Grenadines, said the Caricom Regional Conference on Reparations, which took place this week, hosted by Barbados with the Caricom Reparations Commission (CRC), was key for agreeing a unified strategy to bring Britain to the negotiating table. Gonsalves is now an elder and adviser for the Repair Campaign, a social movement for reparatory justice. He said that slavery happened over centuries and reparations had to be realistic and set over decades. “We need a concrete, multigenerational plan,” he said. On the legal options available to the Caribbean, Gonsalves challenged arguments that Britain did not violate historical laws during transatlantic slavery, adding that the UK’s signature on contemporary UN conventions had established a binding legal obligation for reparative justice.
/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.trail: Leaders hope UK will agree to targeted discussions around reparatory justice, but could consider legal options if Britain resists

/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.headline: How slavery reparations could help make yearning to return to Africa a reality
/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.excerpt: Supporting the right for people of African descent to return to the continent has become a key pillar of the growing global push for reparatory justice from Britain and other colonisers. When Ghana’s president, John Dramani Mahama, visited Jamaica this month he addressed the issue of repatriation for Jamaicans and others whose ancestors were kidnapped from Africa and sold into transatlantic chattel slavery. His visit coincided with a month-long series of emancipation celebrations and came as Jamaican officials prepare to travel to the UK to formally lodge an unprecedented petition with King Charles to seek legal guidance on their slavery reparations claim from Britain. Speaking in Jamaica’s parliament, Mahama described repatriation as “a right of all persons of African descent”. He said this was why Ghana had in 2000 passed the Right of Abode Act, which allows eligible people of African descent to apply for the right to live and work in Ghana without a visa. His country was also “considering a new homeland return bill that will codify residence and citizenship pathways for all members of the global African family”. This was welcomed by the Caribbean reparations movement. Repatriation and resettlement is one of 10 points outlined in the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission’s vision for reparatory justice.
/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.trail: Right for people of African descent to return to continent is key pillar of global push for reparatory justice from colonisers

/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.headline: Man under threat of deportation to Jamaica wins right to rejoin his British family
/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.excerpt: A Jamaican man who has lived more than half his life in the UK and was facing imminent deportation has been allowed to reunite with his British family after a legal challenge. Mark Nelson, 47, came to the UK in 2000 and later set up his own car-mechanic business. He has five British children and a British partner. He faced deportation in 2022 after serving a four-year prison sentence for possession with intent to supply a class B drug, abstracting electricity and two offences of racially aggravated intentional harassment. He had not committed any further offences. The deportation was later cancelled and instead he was tagged and told to report weekly at a Home Office centre. But last month – almost 10 years after his original conviction – Nelson was arrested, detained and told that the government again planned to deport him to Jamaica. The Home Office gave him a ticket for a flight on 7 August, but after reading about his case in the Guardian, lawyers offered to represent him pro bono to challenge his deportation. After they made an 11th-hour application for a judicial review the Home Office backed down on the deportation and cancelled his ticket. This week he was granted bail and can return to the home he shares with his partner, Rachel Derbyshire, in the north of England and see his children again. Nelson said he was overjoyed to to have left the immigration detention centre near Heathrow where he had spent several weeks in hot and crowded conditions.
/world/2026/oct/16/jamaica-slavery-repar.trail: Mark Nelson released from immigration detention on bail after lawyers challenge decision to remove him

/uk-news/2026/oct/16/cloned-number-plate.headline: TfL’s bailiffs are chasing me for a stranger’s unpaid Ulez fines
/uk-news/2026/oct/16/cloned-number-plate.excerpt: Bailiffs turned up at my home to seize goods over four unpaid Ulez fines issued by Transport for London (TfL) that have nothing to do with me. The saga began two months ago when I received four enforcement notices from CDER Group relating to a vehicle I have never owned. I was told my address had been obtained from the DVLA, but the DVLA confirmed that the vehicle has never been registered to me or my address. I sent this confirmation to CDER, but they nevertheless ordered bailiffs to come to my house and told me enforcement could not be stopped. I complained to TfL, which referred me back to CDER. CDER then informed me that TfL had rejected the evidence I had supplied. For more than 25 years I have been repeatedly mistaken for another individual with the same name, resulting in debt collection activity by numerous organisations. I have spent years proving my identity and correcting mistakes, only for the same problems to happen again. CW, Blackpool It seems that the original penalty charge notices (PCNs) were sent to the address of the offending driver and, when they ignored them, tracing agents trawled citizens with the same name and decided you were a good fit. Your labours to prevent bailiffs confiscating your belongings, including sending CDER 13 years of payslips and eight years of bills, took such a toll that you had to be signed off work.
/uk-news/2026/oct/16/cloned-number-plate.trail: Now TFL is threatening to seize goods for four penalties for a car I’ve never owned

/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.headline: France’s class action: inside the 16 October Guardian Weekly
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.excerpt: France has been rocked by huge youth protests in recent weeks over the state of high school education, bringing tens of thousands of people on to the streets. The movement began with outrage over shoddy school conditions in a Paris banlieue, but has spread across the country as pupils voice their anger about a system they say is failing them. For this week’s big story, Paris correspondent Angelique Chrisafis hears from protesters who feel abandoned by the French state. Angelique also looks at the evidence on students’ complaints of dilapidated buildings, teacher shortages, inequality and low investment. Then, Alexander Hurst says fixing the broken education system should be just the start for an aloof political class if it is to finally pay attention to a generation who feel neglected. /world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.trail: What drove student protests? Plus: Duran Duran’s extraordinary world

/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.headline: France’s students are angry about more than crumbling classrooms and missing teachers
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.excerpt: Say what you will about France’s high schools, they still produce world-class slogan writers. Here’s a brief selection spotted during three weeks of blockades and marches over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings: “Pas d’avenir, pas de calme” (No future, no calm). “Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain” (Graduates today, insecure tomorrow). “Vous détruisez notre futur, on bloque votre présent” (You destroy our future, we block your present). A couple more: “Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs” (Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”). “On n’est pas mal éduqués, on n’est pas écoutés” (We’re not badly brought up, we’re just not being listened to). Spot the common theme? The protests, which continued this week with more than 160,000 on the streets on Tuesday, might be over very material problems – but beneath them there clearly lies an altogether more existential worry. This generation fears its future will be one of diminishing prospects, poorly paid, unstable jobs, unaffordable living costs and steadily decaying public infrastructure – the end, in short, of the basic socioeconomic security their parents, mostly, enjoyed. That was the central theme of a 30-second Instagram post I recorded last week with the Guardian’s social media team and that, at time of writing, had been watched almost 540,000 times – with young people in France the largest single group of viewers.
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.trail: Beneath a wave of school protests in France lies an altogether more existential worry: the future prospects of an entire generation

/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.headline: At least 160,000 people take to streets in third week of French school protests
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.excerpt: More than 160,000 schoolchildren, students and trade unionists have marched in cities across France as protests over high school education continued into a third week and many demonstrators denounced policing tactics. Riot police fired teargas at the end of Tuesday’s marches in Nantes and near the Montparnasse area of Paris, but most of the demonstrations over teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling school buildings held in cities including Lyon, Lille and Marseille were peaceful. The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg joined an early morning protest outside the Lycée Paul Éluard in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. “Young people are not being included in the conversation,” said Thunberg, 23, who became famous as a teenager through school strikes demanding action on the climate crisis. As lawyers in their robes formed a human chain to protect pupils after accusations of police brutality, Thunberg said: “Our future is being stolen from us and, as we have seen here, schools are not getting the investment they need.” Students outside the high school said Thunberg had encouraged them to continue with peaceful demonstrations. The protests – backed by trade unionists, some teachers and radical leftwing opposition politicians – have shaken a government caught between calls for urgent public investment and pressure to reduce France’s ballooning deficit and debt.
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.trail: Swedish activist Greta Thunberg joins teenagers calling for investment to fix teacher shortages and crumbling schools

/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.headline: France’s dilemma: protesters demand spending as markets require fiscal restraint
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.excerpt: Eight years have passed since rising fuel prices brought the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) demonstrators to the streets of France, prompting the first big crisis of Emmanuel Macron’s time in the Élysée Palace. As the French president contemplates his exit next year, turmoil has again gripped the streets in the form of student protests, but this time the financial markets are unhappy too. Investors are concerned about the government’s failure to bring spending under control and end a long period of “fiscal incontinence”. Financial markets are unnerved by similar trends in the UK, the US and more recently Italy, causing jitters in global bond markets. But it’s France that has become the biggest worry, hemmed in by debts across the public and private sectors, limiting their scope to dig the country out of a deepening hole. France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% for the UK respectively. In Britain, the chancellor, John Healey, is on course to reduce the budget deficit this year and in 2027. His French counterpart, Roland Lescure, has promised to follow suit after a rise to 5.4% this year, but has yet to say how. ‘I am panicking’ One victim of the uncertainty is business investment. A survey by Medef, France’s largest employer federation, showed 82% of firms were pessimistic about the impact of the next government’s economic policy.
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.trail: Waves of protests expose debt crisis faced by French government, but political wrangling is stalling an escape plan. Is there a way out?

/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.headline: French ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protests
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.excerpt: High school students have again blockaded schools and marched through cities across France, promising to continue their campaign against the poor state of the national education system in the 10th day of protests that have left hundreds injured. Large crowds took to the streets on Thursday for mainly peaceful demonstrations in cities including Lille, Rennes, Nantes, Lyon, Toulon and Marseille, while in Paris a large procession marched through the city centre to the Place de la Bastille. An estimated 25,000 students thronged the square in the east of the capital, with some climbing the monument at its centre, which commemorates France’s 1830 July revolution, while waving the tricolour flag and singing the Marseillaise. As the evening drew in, riot police fired teargas and crowd-dispersal rounds and carried out repeated baton charges to clear the protesters, some of whom hurled bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at the heavily armoured squads. Eliane, 16, a pupil on the Paris march, said she had come to “defend and encourage high schools in an even worse state than mine”, calling the march “magnificent”. She said she planned to continue protesting until concrete progress was achieved. The education minister, Édouard Geffray, told TF1 television on Thursday night that 3,000 substitute teachers would be deployed to about 100 high schools identified as having particularly acute teacher shortages “between tomorrow and Tuesday”.
/world/2026/oct/16/french-police-injurie.trail: Education minister promises 3,000 substitute teachers by Tuesday with schools still blockaded across France

/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.headline: Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.excerpt: Ali Abdulsamed spent all day waiting and walking. Like many people in the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz, he was searching for some food for his family of six. But each time he reached the end of the queue at the grocers, he was greeted with empty shelves. He would go on foot to the next shop, unable to afford the price of petrol, which more than doubled last week. After visiting more than a dozen stores, Abdulsamed managed to find a 25kg bag of wheat flour – sold at more than twice its usual price. It would have to do, he was lucky to find anything at all. As Iran-allied Houthi rebels advance and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces closes off routes into the city, conditions in Taiz have become increasingly difficult. Yemen’s third most populous city has found itself besieged from all sides, with its supplies of fuel, food and other basic goods cut off. The UN World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Monday that the fighting had denied vital assistance to 800,000 people in Taiz: a city of about 1 million, which already had some of the highest levels of food insecurity in the country. The speed of the Houthi advance gave people little time to prepare, prompting a sudden rush on stores and driving up the price of goods still left in the city. Crowds have been gathering around grocery stores and gas stations, trying to stock up on the essentials as fears of shortages spread.
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.trail: Speed of advance has left people rushing to buy food as basic supplies to city are cut off by fighting

/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.headline: Saudi Arabia strikes oil depots in Yemen and says missiles launched toward location of Saudi Aramco HQ
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.excerpt: Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco. The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces. Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure. The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack. Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz. Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen. The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured.
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.trail: Civilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks following deadly strike on Riyadh airport

/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.headline: Saudi Arabia further suspends flights after latest deadly Houthi attack on airport
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.excerpt: Saudi Arabia has been forced to suspend all flights to and from its main international airport in Riyadh until next Saturday after a further round of Houthi missile attacks caused more damage and left one person dead. Some airlines, including Gulf Air, had already said they were cancelling flights until next Saturday. More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said. The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured. Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck. The country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality. But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually. The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises. Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, said Saudi Arabia had invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.” He added: “Markets can diversify suppliers.
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.trail: Energy minister says ‘fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon’ as paramilitary group again breaches stretched defences

/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.headline: Why are the Houthis attacking Saudi airports and how are the missiles getting through?
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.excerpt: What happened over the weekend? On Saturday, a missile strike by the Houthis in Yemen hit Riyadh’s international airport, killing 13 people and wounding hundreds. On Sunday, another attack ‌killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others. CCTV footage showed people cowering at the moment of impact of Saturday’s attack. Footage filmed in the aftermath of showed damage inside one of the terminal buildings at the airport, which is located about 22 miles north of the Saudi Arabian capital. The attacks by the Houthis, an Iran-backed group, were the biggest escalation yet in their campaign ⁠against Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in recent weeks. Though the violence might appear at first sight to be restricted to the Arabian peninsula, it could have global consequences, pushing up fuel prices and so international inflation. Why now? The Houthis’ timing is partly opportunistic but also rooted in the dynamics of the conflicts across the Gulf. The Houthis initially stayed on the sidelines of the conflict launched by the US and Israel against Iran earlier this year. But last month, the Islamist militia movement seized control of key territory and gained virtual control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, which dominates the Red Sea, a critical shipping route for oil and gas exports from the region. The Yemeni government forces and local allies began a major counteroffensive last week to drive back the Houthis from the Bab al-Mandab and also hit other Houthi positions.
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.trail: Attacks by Iran-backed group come amid counteroffensive by Yemeni government supported by Riyadh

/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.headline: Riyadh airport hit again after deadly Houthi missile attack, Saudi authorities say
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.excerpt: A projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport in Riyadh on Sunday, the day after a deadly missile attack on the facility carried out by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebel group killed 13 people. An unidentified projectile hit terminal 4 at King Khalid international airport, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring 11, according to Saudi civil aviation authorities. Air defences also intercepted a cruise missile in the vicinity of the airport. It was the latest of several attacks on the airport in the past week. The escalating attacks threatened to draw more countries into the Yemen conflict and further widen the regional fallout of the US-Iran war, which has already spread to Lebanon and Iraq. In a post on X, the British embassy in Saudi Arabia advised against all but essential travel to the cities of Jeddah and Dammam and to avoid almost all airports. After Saturday’s strike on Riyadh airport, the US president, Donald Trump, said he was weighing whether to join the Saudi military campaign in Yemen, telling reporters: “We’re going to look into it.” The Iran-allied Houthis claimed to have launched several attacks on the airport, including the attack on Saturday, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300 – the deadliest attack on a Gulf country since the war with Iran started in March and an apparent escalation in the Houthis’ war with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government that Riyadh sponsors.
/world/2026/oct/16/future-western-securi.trail: Unidentified projectile strikes King Khalid airport, killing one and injuring 11, as escalating attacks threaten to draw more countries into Yemen conflict

/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.headline: Farage denies Reform would let troops shoot small boats after Jenrick’s ‘lethal force’ claim
/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.excerpt: Nigel Farage has denied that a Reform UK government would authorise lethal force against small boat crossings in the Channel, hours after one of his MPs said the Royal Marines should be permitted to fire on the boats. Farage overruled Robert Jenrick, a Reform UK MP who defected from the Conservatives, who had told TalkTV that the party would deploy the marines to take boats back to France. In a day of party splits where a poll showed the party had fallen to third place behind the Conservatives, the Reform UK chair, Zia Yusuf, also suggested he would not trust Conservative defectors such as Jenrick – and criticised another Reform MP, Suella Braverman, for her suggestions that she could not be considered English because of her ethnicity. The initial row was sparked by Jenrick saying his was the only party prepared to use force against people crossing in small boats. “What we are going to do, and we’re the only political party that has the courage to say this, is deploy the Royal Marines into the Channel. If they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so,” he said. But speaking on LBC, Farage said he would not authorise routine use of force, that it would be used only if soldiers were fired at, and that Jenrick was being “utterly misconstrued”. “Anybody wearing British military uniform who gets fired at has the right to respond. That’s what he was saying,” he said. “Remember, in these camps, every week there are shootings, there are stabbings.
/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.trail: Farage’s intervention comes as Reform chair Zia Yusuf criticises ‘everybody’ in former Tory government that included Jenrick and Suella Braverman

/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.headline: Children and women included in Reform plan to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekers
/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.excerpt: Children and mothers would not be exempt from plans by Reform UK to immediately deport 90,000 asylum seekers and impose a five-year ban on people being granted asylum. The party’s most hardline immigration policies to date were condemned by refugee charities and others as “unworkable” and an abandonment of Britain’s tradition of helping victims of war after they were announced by Nigel Farage on Monday. New claims ⁠would be automatically rejected and failed applicants would be returned either to their home countries or a safe third country while a Reform government would impose tariffs, visa bans or airspace restrictions on countries refusing to accept ‌the return of asylum ‌seekers. Asked if children would be exempt, Farage told a press conference in Kent: “If you allow Palestinian or Afghan women to come as well as children, that may well sound compassionate given the circumstances in that country. However, as soon as you do that you open the door to family reunions, to husbands coming, to partners coming, before you know it you have plenty of young men coming as well.” The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said last month that approximately a quarter of arrivals under the reopened UK Resettlement Scheme (UKRS) will consist of Afghan women and girls fleeing Taliban rule and Palestinians who have fled Gaza. A Home Office source said Farage was mistaken in his claim as those coming under the scheme will not have reunion rights.
/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.trail: Farage’s party says it would ‘embed’ immigration enforcement in UK and use ‘aerial imaging’ to identify people

/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.headline: Revealed: Nigel Farage adviser had unpublicised role at polling firm
/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.excerpt: A close adviser to Nigel Farage had an influential role at a national polling company despite not being publicly associated with the firm, the Guardian can reveal. Chris Bruni-Lowe, Farage’s private pollster for many years, played an important role in the operations of Redfield & Wilton Strategies and used it to develop potential campaign strategies, according to several sources who have worked there. The firm, founded in 2020, is owned by Bruno Rodrigues, a lawyer. Its main public face was Philip van Scheltinga, a Harvard graduate. As the Covid pandemic grew and the UK entered lockdown, the company’s polls received increasing coverage, even while the source of the firm’s polling expertise was unclear. Former employees have now revealed the important role of Bruni-Lowe, who sometimes went by the name “Chris Redfield”, under which quotes were published by the Washington Post newspaper. As well as ordering UK and US voter intention polls, sources said Bruni-Lowe directed research on issues such as council spending, and appeared “obsessed” with producing a dossier which he suggested could be sold to political parties. Bruni-Lowe’s role at the company will amplify questions about transparency in the polling industry, given his longstanding association with Farage at a time of intense scrutiny over the party’s use of polls to shape its political narrative.
/politics/2026/oct/15/farage-accused-pro.trail: Exclusive: Chris Bruni-Lowe used Redfield & Wilton Strategies role to develop potential campaign tactics, sources say

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.headline: Man killed by tiger at Yorkshire zoo had bouts of psychosis, inquest hears
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.excerpt: A man who was killed by a tiger at a South Yorkshire zoo had bouts of psychosis, his family told an inquest opening, as they expressed concerns about his contact with mental health services before his death. William Chapman was mauled to death by the animal at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster on Saturday, after climbing into its enclosure. The park has been closed since the attack but a spokesperson confirmed it would reopen on Friday, and thanked members of the public for “messages of support and love”. The 24-year-old had been diagnosed with schizophrenia but was “highly functioning and independent with no care requirements”, the hearing at Doncaster coroner’s court heard. He was under the care of local mental health services, but the coroner’s officer Caitlin Brookes said his family had expressed “a number of concerns” in relation to his contact with them. Brookes said Rotherham, Doncaster and South Humber NHS foundation trust had launched an investigation after Chapman’s death. The inquest heard Chapman was a self-employed online trader who was living in Doncaster at the time of his death. An initial postmortem found that he had died from multiple traumatic injuries after his encounter with the tiger. The inquest heard he attended Yorkshire Wildlife Park on 10 October, and, at about 1.30pm, climbed over two fences and entered the enclosure housing the 200kg male Siberian tiger named Altai.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.trail: Family express concerns about William Chapman’s contact with mental health services before his death

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.headline: Pensioner pleads guilty to raping woman drugged by husband
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.excerpt: A man from Cheshire has pleaded guilty to the rape of a woman whose husband drugged her and invited other men to sexually assault her while she was unconscious. Graham Brougham, 74, pleaded guilty to rape at a hearing at Manchester Minshull Street crown court on Thursday afternoon. The husband, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his wife, has already admitted to more than 60 offences, and will be sentenced at a later date. The victim sat in the public gallery of the court as Brougham entered his guilty plea. She turned to watch him as he stood in the dock, while a relative sitting beside her held her hand throughout. Brougham, who was set to be the oldest defendant on trial, has been on bail throughout the proceedings, and Judge Greene again granted him bail before sentencing. However, addressing Brougham’s barrister, he said the defendant should not “be under any illusion”, as his “sentence will be custody, and a long time in custody”. Before his arrest Brougham, who lives in Northwich in Cheshire, had played in a 1970s tribute band and was a member of a walking football team. Two other men who were charged alongside the husband have also pleaded guilty at earlier hearings. Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee, a former technician at the city’s university, admitted a number of offences earlier this year, and last month Sean Peers, 38, pleaded guilty to one count of assault by penetration.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.trail: Graham Brougham, 74, was one of a number of men invited to sexually assault victim while she was unconscious

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.headline: Two 1960s London housing estates saved from demolition after decade-long battle
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.excerpt: Two architecturally celebrated council estates in south London that have been under threat of demolition for more than a decade have been saved. Residents of Cressingham Gardens and the Central Hill estate have campaigned tirelessly for their homes to be saved, saying the low-density 1960s developments are significant in design and popular with those living there. Lambeth council argued that the estates were in poor repair and that razing them would create badly needed social and affordable homes. The plans were pursued when Lambeth was controlled by Labour but the Greens won the most seats at elections in May and now run the council as a minority administration. They oppose the demolition plans, which are expected to be reversed at a meeting of the cabinet next week. The fate of the estates attracted wider attention, in part because of their design but also because of the many years of limbo faced by tenants and leaseholders as the council pursued demolition. A 2022 review of Homes Lambeth, the now defunct body which managed housing for the council, questioned the redevelopment plans, saying the net number of social rent homes to be created was very small. Sir Bob Kerslake, the former head of the civil service who led the review, said “feedback was uniformly negative”, with residents of estates earmarked for development citing inconsistent policy, delays and poor communication.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.trail: Change of council leadership hands reprieve to residents of architecturally celebrated developments in Lambeth

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.headline: Severe drought declared in six areas of England as reservoirs run low
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.excerpt: A severe drought has been declared in six areas of England, with some reservoirs at critically low levels, threatening public supplies. Parts of Devon, Cornwall, Dorset, Somerset, East Sussex and West Sussex have moved into severe drought, and urgent measures are being taken to secure public supplies of water after the UK experienced its hottest summer on record. Despite the crisis, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, has yet to approve requests from three water companies, two in areas now in severe drought, to extend restrictions on water use to businesses such as golf clubs and commercial car washes. Emma Hardy, the water minister, indicated on Thursday that the environment could suffer in the continuing drought. Hardy instructed the Environment Agency to prioritise protecting public water supplies in areas affected by severe drought where there is an unavoidable trade-off between environmental rules and water supplies. After a meeting of the national drought group, Eagle, said: “This level of drought is something we have not experienced for decades, so this government is stepping up our support and planning. “We are working closely with water companies to protect public supplies in the areas affected, and I’d continue to urge everyone to think about how they can use water wisely over the coming weeks.” South East Water, South West Water and Southern Water want to impose non-essential user bans on businesses to protect supplies.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.trail: Some reservoirs in south at critical levels as water companies call for extended restrictions that would affect golf clubs, private schools and car washes

/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.headline: No timeline for lifting Land Registry paywall as ownership remains opaque
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.excerpt: The government has refused to say when the public will be able to freely access information about who owns large plots of land across England and Wales. Emma Reynolds, the previous secretary of state for the environment, announced in March that the paywall protecting large amounts of the Land Registry would be partly lifted. Campaigners called for this change in order to make large landowners more accountable, particularly for key areas such as river catchments, grouse moors and peatland. But Reynolds did not put a date on when the paywall would be lifted, and the Land Registry is an “arm’s length body”, a non-ministerial government department that falls under the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. In setting out the land use framework in March, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) pledged only that it would “work with HM Land Registry this year to provide access to free, spatial land ownership data for larger properties covering the vast majority of England and Wales, excluding almost all homeowners”. This may require a further public consultation, in addition to the consultation that preceded the land use framework. In July, a spokesperson for the Land Registry said: “HM Land Registry is supportive of initiatives that promote the more effective use of land. However, our plans with regard to this are still at a very early stage, and a number of aspects will be subject to consultation before any firm decisions are made.
/uk-news/2026/oct/15/russell-brand-jury-.trail: Defra promised in March to work towards free access to data on large plots in England and Wales
